The travelling puppet troupe came to Farhan's village only once a year, setting up behind the panchayat office. This time the lead puppeteer was a woman who had lost her hearing as a child. She worked the strings without a word, and the whole crowd went silent watching a wooden king cry.
Farhan stayed until the lanterns were packed. He asked, through her young assistant Eshaan, how she learned. Eshaan signed the question and laughed at her reply. "She says: by failing for ten years."
All the way home along the canal, Farhan's chest felt too full. That night he cut up an old kurta and made a lopsided puppet from a broom handle. It looked terrible.
He practised with it behind the goat shed every evening for a month.

qa.a: Behind the panchayat office.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel walking home along the canal?
qa.a: He felt deeply moved and inspired; his chest felt too full.

qa.q: How could an adult in Farhan's village encourage this new interest?
qa.a: They could give him cloth and space, watch his shows, and help him write to the troupe to learn more.

qa.q: What might the puppeteer think if she saw Farhan's broom-handle puppet?
qa.a: She might feel touched, remembering her own ten years of failing, and see the start of the same road.

grounding: Shows a teen moved by a role model's art to begin practising it himself.

Pablo had been dragged to the Madrid museum by his school, and for the first hour he looked at his phone. Then his class stopped in front of a huge painting of a bombed town: twisted animals, a screaming mother, a lamp like an eye.
His classmate Chidi nudged him. "You okay?"
Pablo realised he hadn't blinked. "It's like it's still shouting," he said.
The guide explained the painter had made it in a few weeks, furious at a war. Pablo kept thinking: one person, a few weeks, and it still stopped people decades later.
On the bus he opened a notes app and began writing a poem about his grandfather's village, which he had never cared about before. Chidi read it over his shoulder and said, "Keep going."

qa.a: A bombed town: twisted animals, a screaming mother, a lamp like an eye.

qa.q: How did Pablo feel standing in front of the painting?
qa.a: He felt stunned and moved, hardly blinking, as if the painting was still shouting.

qa.q: What could Pablo's teacher do to build on this moment?
qa.a: The teacher could invite students to respond to the painting in their own writing or art and share it in class.

The boys' hostel common room had one old television, and on Sunday evenings the warden, Ramesh sir, showed documentaries whether anyone wanted them or not.
This Sunday it was about a doctor who had walked from village to village for thirty years, treating people for free. Most boys drifted away. Deepak stayed on the torn sofa, knees pulled up.
At the end, the doctor said to the camera, "I was only ever trying to do the next useful thing."
Deepak repeated it under his breath.
Ramesh sir noticed. "You liked it?"
"I don't know if I liked it. I just want to be like that. Not famous. Useful."
Ramesh sir wrote down the name of a weekend first-aid volunteer group on a scrap of paper and handed it to him.

qa.a: "I was only ever trying to do the next useful thing."

Zanele had watched the new boy in her Johannesburg maths class, Sipho, for exactly nine days. She knew he drew spirals in the margins, that he laughed silently with his shoulders, that he had a scar on his thumb. She had decided he was kind, brave, secretly a poet.
Her friend Olga sighed at lunch. "You've never spoken to him."
"I don't need to. I just know."
That afternoon he asked Zanele for a pencil. She handed it over with shaking fingers and couldn't speak. He said thanks and turned back.
Later Olga found her writing his name in tiny letters on her ruler. "Zanele. What if he's just a boy who draws spirals?"
Zanele laughed, but for a second, the thought stung.

In the school library, Kavitha had been pretending to read the same page for twenty minutes. Two tables away, the senior who ran the astronomy club was sorting slides for his talk.
Her friend Tenzin whispered, "You're doing it again."
"Doing what?"
"Staring. You joined astronomy club for him. You don't even like stars."
"I like stars now." Kavitha's cheeks burned. "He said Jupiter has ninety moons like it was poetry."
"He reads that off a slide, Kavi."
She knew it was silly. She had drawn his handwriting in her rough book, planned what she'd say if he ever asked her a question, and imagined whole conversations on the walk home.
When he looked up and smiled at the whole table, her heart hammered for the entire next period.

Dear Tushar,
You're the only person I can tell this to, because you're my cousin and you're three cities away.
There's a boy in my tuition class. I've never had a proper conversation with him. But I've memorised his timetable, the colour of his cycle, and the song he hums before tests. I think about him while brushing my teeth. I write things in my diary that I'd die if anyone read.

Is this normal? Please don't laugh. Actually, you can laugh a little.

I'm Wasim, Ritu's neighbour. We share a wall, so I heard more than I should have last week.
On Monday she was on the phone on the balcony, laughing. On Tuesday the laughing stopped. That night I heard her say, "But you said," and then nothing, then crying that went on a long time.
For three days she didn't come down for badminton. Her mother bought her favourite samosas and left them outside her door. I saw the plate still full the next morning.
On Friday she came down, hair tied tight, eyes puffy, and played badminton like she was angry at the shuttle. She didn't say what happened, and I didn't ask. I just kept passing her the shuttle. At the end she said, "Thanks. Same time tomorrow?"

qa.a: She probably felt worried and helpless, trying to comfort her daughter in a quiet way.

Gurleen, you think I don't understand because I'm old? Listen.
When I was a girl of sixteen, my best friend Harjot suddenly started sitting with other girls. No fight, nothing. Just gone. I, Dilnaz, felt like someone had pulled the floor away. I went to school and came home and cried in the bathroom so my mother wouldn't hear. I didn't eat my lunch for weeks.

Dear diary,
Today I told Keerthana the thing. The real thing. That since Papa left, I pretend at school that everything's normal, and it's exhausting.
I planned it for a week. I nearly backed out three times. My hands were cold. We were sitting on the steps behind the canteen and I said, "Can I tell you something that's not a joke?"
She put her phone away. That was the moment I knew I could.
I talked for maybe ten minutes. She didn't say anything wise. She just said, "That's so heavy. Thank you for telling me." Then she held out half her samosa.
I feel naked and lighter at the same time. Tomorrow I might regret it. Tonight I don't.
Rafiq

After the Holi fair in their small town, Jaya and Rehana sat on the steps of the closed post office, colour still on their arms.
Rehana was talking about the stalls. Jaya kept twisting her dupatta.
"Rehana, you know how I'm always the one who jokes?"
"Yes, you're the joker."
"I don't feel like a joker. Since Dadi died, I feel scared all the time that everyone else will go too. I've never said that out loud."
The silence felt very long. A tractor went past.
Then Rehana leaned her shoulder into Jaya's. "I think about my father's heart all the time," she said quietly. "I never say it either."
They sat until the lamps came on. Jaya's knees had stopped shaking.

His hands started to shake. He felt his breath go short and fast.
Nitin, next to him, said, "Do the thing from PE."

His hands were still a bit unsteady on the burette. But his mind was clear enough to read the scale.

On the night of the village jatra, Yamini climbed the old water tank with her friend Farida instead of watching the drama. Below them the fair glowed; above them the sky was thick with stars she never saw in the town where she studied.
"Do you ever think we're just dust that learned to think?" Yamini said.
Farida laughed. "Only you would say that at a jatra."
"I mean it. Then why does anything matter? Why does Amma pray every morning? Why do I want to be a teacher?"
Farida thought for a while. "Maybe it matters because we're here together for a bit."
Yamini lay back on the cold concrete. She didn't have an answer. But she felt, for a second, very small and very connected, both at once.

Ulla's grandmother died in March, and by June Ulla still hadn't cried at the right times. At the Swedish summer camp, she sat on the jetty every evening, feet in the cold lake, asking herself where people go.
Tuan, the quiet boy from her cabin, sat down one night with a torch. "My family lights incense for our ancestors. My mum says they're still with us."
"Do you believe that?"
"Some days. Other days I think they're just in how we do things. My grandfather folded his shirts a weird way. I do too."
Ulla thought about her grandmother humming while she baked.
"Maybe she's in the humming," Ulla said.
They sat there until the midges came out. It wasn't an answer. It felt like the start of one.

qa.q: Where did Ulla sit every evening?
qa.a: On the jetty, with her feet in the cold lake.

qa.q: How was Ulla feeling at the camp?
qa.a: She felt lost and quietly grieving, unsure where people go after they die.

qa.q: How did Tuan help Ulla think about meaning?
qa.a: He shared his family's belief and his own doubts without pushing, giving Ulla room to find her own idea.

qa.q: What might Tuan be feeling when he talks about his grandfather's shirts?
qa.a: Tuan may feel a warm, slightly shy connection to his grandfather, sharing something private.

grounding: Shows a teen exploring questions about death, connection and meaning with a friend.

In the school's philosophy club, which met in the chemistry lab after hours, the question that Friday was "What is a good life?"
Amandeep said a good life was money and family. Someone else said faith. Anirban, who usually argued with everyone, was quiet.
The teacher asked him directly.
"I don't know," Anirban said. "My father prays. My mother doesn't. They're both good. So maybe it's not what you believe, it's how you live?"
Amandeep frowned. "But then what's the point of believing anything?"
Anirban shrugged. "Maybe believing helps some people live well. I'm still looking for what helps me."
Walking out, Amandeep said, "You're annoying. But I'm going to think about that all weekend."

qa.q: Where did the philosophy club meet?
qa.a: In the chemistry lab after hours.

qa.q: What might Anirban have been feeling before he answered?
qa.a: He may have felt uncertain and thoughtful, still unsure what he believed.

qa.q: How could the teacher build on Anirban's idea next week?
qa.a: The teacher could ask each student to name one way they want to live and what helps them, whatever their belief.

qa.q: How is Amandeep affected by Anirban's answer?
qa.a: Amandeep is frustrated at first but intrigued, saying he'll think about it all weekend.

grounding: Shows teens exploring personal philosophy and spiritual orientation in a school club.

You want to know how I started the blanket drive, Vaibhav? It wasn't planned.
I'm Irfan. Last December I was walking back from tuition and saw a family sleeping under the flyover, kids with no socks. I kept walking. That night I couldn't stop seeing their feet.
So I asked my building's group if anyone had old blankets. Three people replied. Then my mother made me go door to door. Terrible. Knocking on aunties' doors. But we got forty blankets.
We took them with the local shelter's volunteers, not on our own. The shelter manager said what people actually needed was socks and rice more than blankets. That taught me something.
This year I'm asking the shelter first what they need. Then we collect.

qa.q: How many blankets did they collect?
qa.a: Forty blankets.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel after walking past the family?
qa.a: Irfan felt uneasy and guilty, unable to stop seeing the children's feet that night.

qa.q: What did Irfan learn about helping well?
qa.a: To ask the shelter what people need first, instead of guessing, and to go with the shelter's volunteers.

qa.q: What might the shelter manager feel about young volunteers like Irfan?
qa.a: The manager may feel grateful and glad to guide eager helpers toward what really helps.

grounding: A teen describes turning discomfort about homelessness into a considered volunteer effort.

I'm Kalyani, Gurpreet's classmate. Since the monsoon, she has been different.
It started when a boy in our class who uses a wheelchair couldn't get to the new science lab on the second floor. Everyone felt bad for a day. Gurpreet didn't stop at a day.
She wrote a letter to the principal and got twenty signatures. When nothing happened, she measured the stairs, found out about ramps, and presented to the school council with photos.
Some people called her a show-off. She kept going, quietly. I don't know if she's doing it for him or for herself or both.
Last week the school moved his class's labs to the ground floor. Gurpreet just said, "Good," and went back to her book. But she was smiling at the page.

qa.q: How many signatures did Gurpreet get?
qa.a: Twenty signatures.

qa.q: What does Gurpreet smiling at her book suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt quietly satisfied and relieved that the change finally happened.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet do that made her effort work?
qa.a: She kept going after the first letter failed, gathered facts and photos, and used the school council.

qa.q: How does Kalyani see Gurpreet's campaign?
qa.a: Kalyani admires the persistence but admits she isn't sure of Gurpreet's reasons.

grounding: A classmate observes a teen campaign steadily for a peer who uses a wheelchair.

First Saturday: Kishore joined the neighbourhood reading circle for younger kids only because his mother pushed him. He sat at the back of the community hall, bored, while Minakshi didi read to eight children.
Two weeks later: one small boy, who spoke mostly Bhojpuri and was teased for it, wouldn't read aloud. Kishore, whose grandmother spoke Bhojpuri, sat beside him and whispered the words in both languages. The boy read a whole page. The others clapped.
A month on: Kishore arrived early, arranged the mats, and asked Minakshi didi if they could add books in other languages. "Some of these kids are made to feel small for how they talk at home," he said. "Not here." He brought three books from his grandmother's shelf.

qa.q: What did Kishore bring from his grandmother's shelf?
qa.a: Three books.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel at the first Saturday?
qa.a: He felt bored and reluctant, sitting at the back only because his mother pushed him.

qa.q: How could Minakshi didi support Kishore's new commitment?
qa.a: She could give him a regular role, like helping kids who speak other languages, and include his book ideas.

qa.q: How might the small boy feel after reading a whole page?
qa.a: He likely felt proud and accepted, especially after being teased for how he talks.

grounding: Shows a teen's service growing from reluctance into standing up for a marginalised child.

"Parul, come fast, everyone's jumping off the canal bridge!" Parveen shouted from the gate.
Parul grabbed her slippers. "Wait, how deep is it?"
"Who cares, it's so hot! Everyone's doing it."
Parul's heart was already racing. She could hear the shrieks from the road. Her feet wanted to run.
"Parveen, stop. Did anyone check the water after last week's rain?"
"Stop being boring."
Parul stood still, breathing. "Let's go and look first. If it's too fast, we sit on the bank and eat mangoes. I'm not jumping blind."
At the bridge the water was brown and fast. Two boys were already coughing on the bank. Parul called her uncle, who came and told everyone to get out, and the kids moved to the shallow steps.

qa.q: What was everyone doing at the canal?
qa.a: Jumping off the canal bridge.

qa.q: How did Parul feel when she first heard the shouts?
qa.a: She felt excited and tempted; her heart raced and her feet wanted to run.

qa.q: What helped Parul make a cooler choice?
qa.a: She stopped, breathed and asked about the water, then went to look before deciding, and called her uncle when it was unsafe.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel after seeing the coughing boys?
qa.a: Parveen may feel shaken and relieved that Parul slowed them down.

grounding: Shows a teen pausing under excitement and peer pressure to make a safer decision.

passage:
Last year I almost quit the football team in the middle of a match. I'm Vijay, and I still get hot in the face thinking about it.
The referee gave a penalty against us that I was sure was wrong. Bhupen, our striker, started shouting, and I shouted too. Then I ripped off my captain's armband and threw it on the grass. Everyone stared.
Coach didn't yell. He picked up the band and said, "Sit for five minutes. Then decide."
In those five minutes my breathing slowed. I saw my teammates' faces. I felt ashamed.
I went back on. We lost anyway. But I learned that when I'm boiling, my choices aren't really mine yet. Now I count to ten and look at the sky before I say anything in a match.

qa.q: What did Vijay throw on the grass?
qa.a: The captain's armband.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel after sitting for five minutes?
qa.a: Vijay felt ashamed once the anger cooled and the teammates' faces came into view.

qa.q: What did the coach do that helped?
qa.a: He stayed calm and gave Vijay five minutes before deciding, letting the heat pass before a choice was made.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have seen Vijay's outburst?
qa.a: Bhupen may have felt partly responsible for starting the shouting, and surprised at how far Vijay went.

grounding: A teen recalls a heated decision in a match and learning to wait until the anger cooled.

Tuition teacher's note on Parul, Class 12
Parul came in on Tuesday furious. Her friend Ritu had told her that a group of girls laughed at her dance video. Parul wanted to post a reply video mocking them, right then.
I asked her to write the post in her notebook instead of her phone and wait until after the maths test. She was annoyed, but agreed.
After the test she read it back and winced. "That's so mean. They'd just screenshot it."
Ritu said the same. Parul tore out the page.
We talked about how anger makes everything feel urgent. She suggested her own rule: nothing gets posted when she's upset, only the next morning. I told her I'd ask about it next week.
She left calmer, still hurt, but in charge of it.

qa.q: What did Parul want to post?
qa.a: A reply video mocking the girls.

qa.q: How did Parul feel when she read the post back after the test?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and uncomfortable, wincing at how mean it sounded.

qa.q: Which step by the teacher helped, and what comes next?
qa.a: The teacher slowed Parul down by having her write it on paper and wait, and plans to check in next week on her own rule.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel about Parul's decision?
qa.a: Ritu may feel relieved, since telling Parul could otherwise have made things worse.

grounding: A teacher records a teen learning to delay a heated choice until she cools down.
